archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (goaltending-sunk)
archetype.definition: A Kings team that splits five-on-five play about evenly with opponents but has its record dragged near the bottom of the league by poor goaltending, a broken penalty kill, cold finishing and bad luck in close games.

report.headline: A league-average five-on-five team buried by its goaltending, penalty kill and finishing.
report.take:
At 5-11-2 and 30th of 32 on the site, Los Angeles looks like a lottery team. Its five-on-five play says something else. The Kings own 50.6% of the expected goals and 51% of the shot attempts, both a touch above the league line, and they put 28.2 shots a game on net, 12th in the league, while allowing 27, which is 15th. A team that shoots and defends like that is ordinary, not bad. The gap between that profile and a 55-point pace is the story of this season.

Three things open the gap, and none of them is shot volume. The first is goaltending. The Goalies GSAx of -8.9 ranks 29th, and nearly all of it belongs to Darcy Kuemper: an .873 save % and -7.4 GSAx over 11 starts. Anton Forsberg has been roughly average in his seven, at .908 and 0.2. The second is the penalty kill, at 67.2%, 29th and more than ten points under the league's 77.4%. The third is finishing. The skaters convert 9.7% of their shots, 27th, against a league mean of 11.4%. Alex Laferriere, for one, has 3 goals on 55 shots. Add a Pts vs Goal Diff of -3.6, 30th, and the Kings have lost nearly every coin flip available to them.

The numbers do hide a real problem, and it is depth. The top of the lineup drives play. Artemi Panarin has 19 points and a .608 xGF %, Adrian Kempe sits at .598, Laferriere at .578, and Brandt Clarke is at .597 from the back end. Below that the bottom six gets buried: Erik Haula at .399, Scott Laughton at .423, Trevor Moore at .453. The defense also bleeds to centers, allowing 3.83 points a game to them, 27th. Forwards graded D- and a blueline graded D are not only bad luck. Some of the losing is earned.

History supports both readings. Two seasons ago this was a 105-point team with the league's second-best defense and +10.9 GSAx. Last season the offense fell to 29th and a +5.6 Pts vs Goal Diff carried a thin team to 90 points. This year the scoring is still weak and the luck has flipped. The underlying shot share has slid from 55.2% xGF two years ago to 50.6% now. Expect the Kings to play closer to .500 hockey from here if the crease steadies. They have already given away too much ground to count on climbing back into a playoff spot.

strengths.title: They still win the shot battle
strengths.body: The Kings hold 50.6% of expected goals and 51% of shot attempts at five-on-five, and they outshoot opponents 28.2 to 27 a game. That process tends to persist, and it is why the results should improve once save % and shooting % drift back toward normal. It has eroded from earlier seasons, though, so it is a floor rather than an edge.

strengths.title: Panarin-Kempe-Laferriere top group drives play
strengths.body: Panarin has 19 points in 17 games with a .608 xGF %, and Kempe and Laferriere are both near .600. That top group, with Clarke's 13 points from the blueline, is outplaying opponents and producing on the power play, which runs at 21.7%, near league average. The scoring from this group is real. Laferriere's finishing should rise.

concerns.title: Kuemper's save percentage is sinking them
concerns.body: The team's .887 save % ranks 23rd and its GSAx ranks 29th. Most of that is Kuemper at .873 and -7.4 GSAx, while Forsberg has held average. Some of it should regress, but the F goaltending grade is the single biggest reason the record trails the play. Until the starts tilt or Kuemper recovers, the Kings will keep giving away games they control.

concerns.title: A penalty kill near the bottom
concerns.body: At 67.2% the PK ranks 29th, more than ten points under the league average. Poor goaltending feeds that number, so part of it will heal with the save %. Still, a kill this far off costs goals almost every week, and last season's 74.6% shows it was already slipping.

concerns.title: Bottom six gets outplayed badly
concerns.body: Haula, Laughton and Moore all sit well under 50% xGF, and opposing centers score freely against this team, which ranks 27th in points allowed to them. Unlike the goaltending and shooting luck, this is a talent and structure issue that will not simply regress away. It is behind the D- forward grade.

trend.note: A rough October was followed by a worse November: 1-4 in the last five, closing with four straight home losses. Over the last 10, though, the scoring is up slightly on the season rate, so the slide is more about results than collapsing play.

weekAhead.headline: Four road games against three winners; their power plays are the opening.
weekAhead.body:
All four games are on the road, and three come against teams with winning records: Boston (13-6-1, 5th on the site), Ottawa (13-6-2) and Montréal (12-4-4). Boston is the hardest test, a top-five defense with a .911 save % and +10.9 GSAx. Its 104.2 PDO says some of that is running hot, but it will not cool on the Kings' schedule. Toronto (8-12-2) is the clear opportunity. It is 27th in xGF % and owns a Pts vs Goal Diff even worse than LA's.

The schedule does offer a quiet break for the Kings' biggest weakness. Ottawa's power play ranks 32nd and Montréal's 31st, and Boston's is 25th, so the 67.2% penalty kill should be tested less than usual. The exception is Toronto, which converts at 26.7%, sixth in the league. Ottawa and Montréal are both riding positive Pts vs Goal Diff and PDO numbers, so they are beatable for a team that controls play. Even so, two wins on this trip would be a good week.

keyMatchups.title: Kings' PK vs Toronto's power play
keyMatchups.body: Toronto's power play ranks sixth at 26.7%, and LA's kill is 29th. Otherwise this is the softest game of the week, against a team that gets outchanced at five-on-five. Staying out of the box is how the Kings win it.

keyMatchups.title: LA's wingers against soft wing coverage
keyMatchups.body: Toronto and Ottawa both allow wingers more points than expected, ranking 24th and 22nd. That suits a team whose best producers, Panarin, Kempe and Laferriere, play on the wing. If the finishing slump breaks this week, it should start in those two games.

keyMatchups.title: Boston's hot goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Boston's goalies are fourth in GSAx at +10.9 and third in save %, the mirror image of LA's crease. The Kings' shot volume will matter less in that game than whether their own goalie keeps it close.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal. Forsberg's .908 against Kuemper's .873 is the difference between a competitive trip and another lost week.

restOfSeason.body:
The Kings' process is roughly average and their results are among the league's worst, and that gap should narrow. Shooting at 9.7%, a 98.7 PDO and a -3.6 Pts vs Goal Diff all tend to drift back. With even league-average goaltending, this is close to a .500 points team the rest of the way. That projects to about 68-80 standings points and 28-35 wins, well above the current 55-point pace.

What will not regress on its own is the thin bottom six, the weakness against centers and a penalty kill that was already declining last year. Those are why the ceiling is modest. Even with a strong recovery, the hole from 5-11-2 in a division where Edmonton and Vegas are pulling away makes the playoffs a long shot rather than a realistic target. Expect goals allowed to settle somewhere around 3.0-3.3 a game if the save % normalizes.
swingFactors: Kuemper's save % or a shift of starts to Forsberg
Penalty kill recovering toward league average
Bottom-six forwards breaking even at five-on-five

confidence.note: 18 games is a small sample, but shot-share and save-% splits point clearly one way.
